title: Uniprocessor Mixed-Criticality Scheduling with Graceful Degradation by Completion Rate

extraction.paper_name: Uniprocessor Mixed-Criticality Scheduling with Graceful Degradation by Completion Rate
extraction.paper_description: This paper introduces a novel mixed-criticality (MC) system model that guarantees graceful degradation for LO-criticality tasks in HI mode, specified by minimum cumulative completion rates (r_i). It proposes an admission control procedure, an EDF-GVD scheduler with virtual deadlines, and a pseudo-polynomial time demand-bound-function-based schedulability test. Additionally, it provides a theoretical analysis for the maximum time duration required for the system to switch back from HI to LO mode.

formal_description.statement: tau_i = {C_i, T_i, D_i, r_i, chi_i} , forall tau_i in tau_LO

variables.C_i: Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) estimation for task tau_i
variables.r_i: Minimum cumulative admission rate for task tau_i in HI mode
variables.chi_i: Criticality level of task tau_i, which is LO (Lower Criticality)
variables.tau_LO: The set of all LO-criticality tasks

assumptions: Each task generates an infinite number of MC jobs
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the parameters characterizing a LO-criticality task in the proposed MC system model.

informal_sketch.intuition: LO-criticality tasks are less important but still need some guarantees. They have a single WCET estimate, a period, a deadline, and a special 'completion rate' (r_i) that dictates how many of their jobs must be completed if the system enters HI mode.
steps: Identify a task tau_i as LO-criticality (chi_i = LO).
Assign its standard real-time parameters: C_i (execution time), T_i (release period), D_i (deadline).
Assign a new parameter r_i, representing the minimum fraction of jobs that must complete in HI mode.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class LO_Task:
    def __init__(self, C, T, D, r):
        self.C = C
        self.T = T
        self.D = D
        self.r = r
        self.chi = 'LO'
key_insights: Introduces 'r_i' as a new parameter for LO-criticality tasks, enabling graceful degradation.
LO tasks have only one WCET estimate, C_i.

formal_description.statement: tau_i = {C_LO_i, C_HI_i, T_i, D_i, chi_i} , forall tau_i in tau_HI .

variables.C_LO_i: LO-criticality Worst-Case Execution Time (LO-WCET) estimation for task tau_i
variables.C_HI_i: HI-criticality Worst-Case Execution Time (HI-WCET) estimation for task tau_i
variables.chi_i: Criticality level of task tau_i, which is HI (Higher Criticality)
variables.tau_HI: The set of all HI-criticality tasks

assumptions: Each task generates an infinite number of MC jobs
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the parameters characterizing a HI-criticality task in the proposed MC system model.

informal_sketch.intuition: HI-criticality tasks are the most important and have two WCET estimates: an optimistic one (C_LO_i) for normal operation and a pessimistic one (C_HI_i) for when things go wrong. They must always meet their deadlines.
steps: Identify a task tau_i as HI-criticality (chi_i = HI).
Assign its standard real-time parameters: T_i (release period), D_i (deadline).
Assign two WCET estimates: C_LO_i (used in LO mode) and C_HI_i (used in HI mode).
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class HI_Task:
    def __init__(self, C_LO, C_HI, T, D):
        self.C_LO = C_LO
        self.C_HI = C_HI
        self.T = T
        self.D = D
        self.chi = 'HI'
key_insights: HI tasks have two WCET estimates, reflecting different levels of assurance.
Their deadlines must be met in both LO and HI modes.

formal_description.statement: Under LO mode, each task tau_i signals its completion upon receiving an execution length no more than C_LO_i (for HI tasks) or C_i (for LO tasks), and all jobs complete on or before their deadlines.

variables.C_i: WCET of a LO-criticality task tau_i
variables.C_LO_i: LO-WCET of a HI-criticality task tau_i

assumptions: System is operating in LO mode
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the conditions for a correct schedule when the system is in LO mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: In LO mode, the system operates under normal, optimistic conditions. All tasks are expected to finish within their smaller WCET estimates, and all deadlines must be met.
steps: For HI-criticality tasks: jobs must complete within C_LO_i.
For LO-criticality tasks: jobs must complete within C_i.
All jobs (both HI and LO) must complete by their respective deadlines D_i.
key_insights: All tasks are guaranteed in LO mode.
HI tasks use their optimistic C_LO_i estimates.

formal_description.statement: Under HI mode, each HI-criticality task tau_i may receive an execution up to C_HI_i, while LO-criticality jobs will nevertheless be executed at a minimum cumulative admission rate r_i. In other words, starting from the last HI mode switch point, out of any N in Z+ consecutive jobs released by any LO-criticality task tau_i, r_i * N jobs are guaranteed to receive full execution (between their release time and the deadlines).

variables.C_HI_i: HI-WCET of a HI-criticality task tau_i
variables.r_i: Minimum cumulative admission rate for a LO-criticality task tau_i
variables.N: Any positive integer representing a number of consecutive job releases

assumptions: System is operating in HI mode (triggered by a HI-criticality task overrunning its C_LO_i)
LO-criticality jobs are subject to an admission control procedure
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the conditions for a correct schedule when the system is in HI mode, including graceful degradation for LO tasks.

informal_sketch.intuition: In HI mode, the system is under stress (a HI task overran its C_LO_i). HI tasks are given more resources (up to C_HI_i) and must still meet deadlines. LO tasks are degraded but not completely dropped; a minimum fraction of their jobs (r_i) must still complete.
steps: For HI-criticality tasks: jobs may execute up to C_HI_i and must complete by their deadlines.
For LO-criticality tasks: for any N consecutive jobs released, at least r_i * N jobs must be admitted and complete by their deadlines.
Dropped LO-criticality jobs do not consume resources.
key_insights: HI tasks are fully guaranteed, using their pessimistic WCETs.
LO tasks are guaranteed a minimum service level (r_i) rather than being completely dropped, providing graceful degradation.

formal_description.statement:
foreach tau_i in tau_LO do a_i = 0; end
while true do
    if j_b in tau_i released then
        if (a_i < b * r_i) then
            // schedule j_b using EDF
            a_i = a_i + 1;
        else
            // The job j_b is dropped
        end
    end
end

variables.tau_LO: The set of all LO-criticality tasks
variables.a_i: Counter for the number of jobs of task tau_i that have been admitted and executed
variables.j_b: The b-th job instance of task tau_i
variables.b: The index of the current job instance (e.g., 1st, 2nd, 3rd, ...)
variables.r_i: The minimum cumulative admission rate for task tau_i

assumptions: Jobs are released sequentially and their index 'b' is known
formal_description.conclusion: A dynamic procedure to decide which LO-criticality jobs to admit for execution in HI mode, ensuring the minimum cumulative admission rate r_i is met.

informal_sketch.intuition: To guarantee a minimum completion rate r_i for LO-criticality tasks in HI mode, this algorithm dynamically decides whether to admit a newly released job or drop it. It does this by keeping a running count of admitted jobs and comparing it against the required cumulative rate.
steps: Initialize a counter `a_i` to 0 for each LO-criticality task `tau_i` to track admitted jobs.
When the `b`-th job (`j_b`) of `tau_i` is released:
Check if the current count of admitted jobs (`a_i`) is less than `b * r_i` (the minimum required admitted jobs up to this point).
If `a_i < b * r_i`, admit `j_b` for scheduling (e.g., using EDF) and increment `a_i`.
Otherwise, drop `j_b`.
key_insights: Ensures the cumulative admission rate `r_i` is maintained over any sequence of jobs.
Provides a concrete mechanism for graceful degradation.
Minimizes consecutive drops by distributing admitted jobs.

variables.S_tau_i: The maximum number of consecutive jobs of task tau_i that can be dropped
variables.r_i: The minimum cumulative admission rate for task tau_i

assumptions: The admission control procedure (Algorithm 1) is used for LO-criticality tasks in HI mode
r_i is a rational number (or can be approximated)
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a formula to calculate the maximum number of consecutive drops for a LO-criticality task while still satisfying its minimum cumulative admission rate r_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task needs to complete, for example, 1 out of every 2 jobs (r_i = 0.5), then at most 1 job can be dropped consecutively. If it needs 1 out of 4 (r_i = 0.25), then at most 3 can be dropped. This formula generalizes that relationship.
steps: Consider `r_i` as a fraction `m_i / k_i` in its simplest form (e.g., 0.5 = 1/2, 0.25 = 1/4).
The admission control ensures that `m_i` jobs are admitted out of any `k_i` consecutive jobs.
The maximum number of consecutive drops occurs when `m_i` jobs are admitted, and then `k_i - m_i` jobs are dropped.
Since `r_i = m_i / k_i`, we have `k_i = m_i / r_i`.
Substitute `k_i` into the drops formula: `S_tau_i = (m_i / r_i) - m_i = m_i * (1 / r_i - 1)`.
To minimize `S_tau_i` for a given `r_i`, we take `m_i = 1` (the smallest possible numerator for the fraction `r_i` in its simplest form).
key_insights: The admission control strategy is designed to spread out admitted jobs, minimizing consecutive drops.
The formula quantifies this minimum, which is important for applications sensitive to bursty degradation.

variables.dbf_LO_LO: Demand bound function for a LO-criticality task in LO mode

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum execution demand of a LO-criticality task tau_i within any time interval of length delta, assuming the system is in LO mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: In LO mode, LO-criticality tasks behave like standard sporadic tasks. This function calculates the worst-case total execution time required by jobs of task tau_i that are released and must complete within a given time window delta.
steps: Determine the number of jobs of task `tau_i` whose release times and deadlines fall within the interval `delta`.
This is calculated as `floor((delta - D_i) / T_i) + 1`.
Multiply this number by the task's WCET `C_i` to get the total demand.
key_insights: This is the classical demand bound function for a single sporadic task.
It assumes all jobs of `tau_i` will execute for their full `C_i`.

variables.dbf_LO_HI: Demand bound function for a HI-criticality task in LO mode

assumptions: Virtual deadlines D_v_i are assigned to HI-criticality tasks
formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum execution demand of a HI-criticality task tau_i within any time interval of length delta, considering its LO-WCET and virtual deadline, assuming the system is in LO mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: In LO mode, HI-criticality tasks are scheduled using their optimistic WCET (C_LO_i) but with an earlier 'virtual deadline' (D_v_i). This function calculates their demand based on these modified parameters.
steps: Determine the number of jobs of task `tau_i` whose release times and *virtual* deadlines fall within the interval `delta`.
This is calculated as `floor((delta - D_v_i) / T_i) + 1`.
Multiply this number by the task's LO-WCET `C_LO_i` to get the total demand.
key_insights: Virtual deadlines effectively 'pull forward' the demand of HI-criticality tasks in LO mode.
This creates slack for potential overruns and mode switches to HI mode.

formal_description.statement: sum_{tau_i in tau} dbf(tau_i, delta) <= delta, forall delta >= 0.

variables.dbf(tau_i, delta): The demand bound function for task tau_i over an interval of length delta

formal_description.conclusion: A constrained-deadline task set tau can be successfully scheduled by EDF on a uniprocessor if and only if the total demand of all tasks in any time interval delta does not exceed the length of that interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: This is a fundamental principle of EDF scheduling. If, at any point, the total amount of computation required by jobs that must complete by a certain time `t` exceeds the available processor time `t`, then a deadline miss is inevitable. The demand bound function (DBF) calculates this worst-case demand.
steps: For every possible time interval length `delta` (up to a known bound):
Calculate the demand `dbf(tau_i, delta)` for each task `tau_i` in the system.
Sum these individual demands to get the `total_demand` for the interval `delta`.
Check if `total_demand <= delta`.
If this condition holds for all relevant `delta` values, the task set is EDF schedulable.
key_insights: The demand bound function (DBF) provides a worst-case measure of processor demand.
The condition `sum(dbf) <= delta` is a necessary and sufficient test for EDF schedulability on a uniprocessor for constrained-deadline tasks.

formal_description.statement: dbf_HI_LO(tau_i, delta) = C_i * Num_i(floor((delta - D_i) / T_i) + 1)

variables.dbf_HI_LO: Demand bound function for a LO-criticality task in HI mode
variables.Num_i(x): Maximum number of jobs of task tau_i that are selected to execute among any x consecutive jobs

assumptions: Carry-over jobs of LO-criticality tasks are dropped upon mode switch
formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum execution demand of a LO-criticality task tau_i within any time interval of length delta, considering only jobs released after the mode switch and subject to admission control.

informal_sketch.intuition: In HI mode, LO-criticality tasks are subject to the admission control procedure (Algorithm 1). This demand function calculates the worst-case execution time required by *admitted* jobs of task tau_i whose deadlines fall within the interval delta.
steps: First, determine the maximum number of jobs of `tau_i` that *could* be released and have deadlines within `delta` if all were admitted: `potential_jobs = floor((delta - D_i) / T_i) + 1`.
Then, use the `Num_i(x)` function to find out how many of these `potential_jobs` would actually be admitted by the admission control policy.
Multiply this number of admitted jobs by the task's WCET `C_i` to get the total demand.
key_insights: This demand function directly incorporates the effect of the admission control policy.
It ensures that only the demand from jobs guaranteed by `r_i` is considered.

formal_description.statement: forall x >= 0, Num_i(x) = r_i * x under the admission control procedure described in Sec. III.

variables.x: Number of consecutive jobs of task tau_i
variables.Num_i(x): Number of jobs of task tau_i admitted among x consecutive jobs
variables.r_i: Minimum cumulative admission rate for task tau_i

assumptions: The admission control procedure (Algorithm 1) is strictly followed for LO-criticality tasks in HI mode.
formal_description.conclusion: The admission control procedure guarantees that, for any sequence of x consecutive jobs of a LO-criticality task tau_i, exactly r_i * x jobs will be admitted for execution.

informal_sketch.intuition: The admission control algorithm (Algorithm 1) is designed to maintain a cumulative admission rate. This lemma formally proves that this mechanism ensures the rate `r_i` is met not just asymptotically, but for any finite window of `x` consecutive jobs.
steps: The proof uses a contradiction argument.
Assume there exists a window of `x` jobs where more than `r_i * x` jobs are admitted.
Let `num(p, q)` be the number of jobs admitted from the `p`-th to `q`-th job.
Algorithm 1 ensures `num(1, b) = floor(b * r_i)` (or similar, depending on exact interpretation of `a_i < b * r_i`). The paper states `r_i * x` directly.

If `num(y+1, y+x) > r_i * x`, then there must be a job `j_b` (where `b` is between `y+1` and `y+x`) that was admitted, but its admission would violate the `a_i < b * r_i` condition when considering all jobs from the start.

Specifically, if the `b`-th job is admitted, then `num(1, b-1) < (b-1) * r_i`. But if `num(y+1, y+x)` is too high, it implies `num(1, b-1)` would have been `b * r_i` or more, leading to a contradiction.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def Num_i(x, r_i):
    # This function represents the outcome of Algorithm 1
    # The lemma states that for any x, the number of admitted jobs is r_i * x
    # (assuming r_i * x can be fractional, or implies floor/ceil for integer counts)
    return r_i * x
key_insights: This lemma is crucial because it quantifies the exact number of admitted jobs, allowing for precise demand bound calculations.
It demonstrates the strong guarantee provided by the admission control, not just an asymptotic rate.

variables.full: Full demand of a HI-criticality task in HI mode

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum execution demand of a HI-criticality task tau_i within any time interval of length delta, assuming all jobs (including a potential carry-over job) execute for their full HI-WCET.

informal_sketch.intuition: When the system is in HI mode, HI-criticality tasks are guaranteed to execute up to their pessimistic WCET (C_HI_i). This function calculates the total demand from such tasks, considering the impact of virtual deadlines on the timing of a 'carry-over' job (a job released before mode switch but completing after).
steps: The term `(D_i - D_v_i)` represents the 'slack' or difference between the actual deadline and the virtual deadline.
This slack is used to adjust the interval `delta` to correctly count jobs that contribute to demand in HI mode, especially for a carry-over job.
Calculate the number of jobs whose effective deadlines (considering the `D_i - D_v_i` adjustment) fall within `delta`.
Multiply this number by `C_HI_i`.
key_insights: Accounts for the full, pessimistic execution time of HI tasks in HI mode.
The `(D_i - D_v_i)` term is critical for correctly handling the demand of a job that might have started in LO mode and continued into HI mode.

formal_description.statement: done(tau_i, delta) = max{0, C_LO_i - rho + D_i - D_v_i} if D_i > rho >= D_i - D_v_i, else 0. Where rho = delta mod T_i.

variables.done: Minimum amount of work of the carry-over job of task tau_i that must have finished in LO mode
variables.rho: The remainder of delta divided by T_i (delta % T_i)

assumptions: This function is used to adjust the demand of a carry-over job
formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the minimum amount of execution that a carry-over job of task tau_i (a job released before mode switch but with deadline after) must have completed in LO mode, to avoid overcounting its demand in HI mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: When the system switches from LO to HI mode, a HI-criticality job might be partially executed. This function estimates how much of that job's `C_LO_i` execution *must have already completed* before the mode switch, so that this 'done' work is not counted again as demand in HI mode.
steps: Calculate `rho = delta % T_i`, which represents the time elapsed since the last period boundary within the interval `delta`.

Check a specific condition: `D_i > rho >= D_i - D_v_i`. This condition identifies a scenario where a carry-over job's timing (release, virtual deadline, actual deadline) aligns in a way that allows for a specific calculation of 'done' work.

If the condition holds, the 'done' work is `max(0, C_LO_i - rho + D_i - D_v_i)`. This complex term accounts for the portion of `C_LO_i` that must have been completed by the mode switch, considering the virtual deadline's effect.
Otherwise, if the condition does not hold, no specific 'done' work is guaranteed, so it's 0.
key_insights: This function is crucial for accurately calculating demand in HI mode by preventing overcounting of work already performed in LO mode by a carry-over job.
It's a specific adjustment for the demand bound function in mixed-criticality contexts.

formal_description.statement: dbf_HI_HI(tau_i, delta) = full(tau_i, delta) - done(tau_i, delta)

variables.dbf_HI_HI: Demand bound function for a HI-criticality task in HI mode
variables.full(tau_i, delta): Full demand of task tau_i in HI mode
variables.done(tau_i, delta): Minimum amount of work of the carry-over job of task tau_i that must have finished in LO mode

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the maximum execution demand of a HI-criticality task tau_i within any time interval of length delta, correctly accounting for the full HI-WCET and subtracting any work already completed by a carry-over job in LO mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total demand of a HI-criticality task in HI mode is its 'full' demand (assuming all jobs execute for their C_HI_i) minus any work that was already 'done' by a carry-over job in LO mode. This prevents double-counting and provides an accurate demand bound.
steps: Calculate the `full(tau_i, delta)` demand, which assumes all jobs execute for `C_HI_i`.
Calculate the `done(tau_i, delta)` amount, which is the minimum work completed by a carry-over job in LO mode.
Subtract `done(tau_i, delta)` from `full(tau_i, delta)` to get the net demand for `tau_i` in HI mode.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def dbf_HI_HI(tau_i, delta):
    return full(tau_i, delta) - done(tau_i, delta)
key_insights: This function combines the pessimistic demand calculation with an adjustment for pre-executed work.
It's essential for accurate schedulability analysis of HI tasks in HI mode.

results.identifier: Theorem 1: MC Schedulability Test for EDF-GVD

formal_description.statement:
A mixed-criticality system tau can be successfully scheduled by EDF-GVD on a uniprocessor if both of the following conditions hold.
(A): sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} dbf_LO_LO(tau_i, delta) + sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} dbf_LO_HI(tau_i, delta) <= delta, forall delta >= 0.
(B): sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} dbf_HI_LO(tau_i, delta) + sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} dbf_HI_HI(tau_i, delta) <= delta, forall delta >= 0.

variables.dbf_LO_LO: Demand bound function for LO-criticality tasks in LO mode
variables.dbf_LO_HI: Demand bound function for HI-criticality tasks in LO mode (with virtual deadlines)
variables.dbf_HI_LO: Demand bound function for LO-criticality tasks in HI mode (with admission control)
variables.dbf_HI_HI: Demand bound function for HI-criticality tasks in HI mode (with HI-WCETs and carry-over handling)

assumptions: Virtual deadlines (D_v_i) for HI-criticality tasks are appropriately set (e.g., using Algorithm 2)
formal_description.conclusion: The mixed-criticality system is schedulable, meaning all correctness criteria (LO mode and HI mode) are satisfied.

informal_sketch.intuition: To guarantee schedulability for a mixed-criticality system with graceful degradation, we must ensure that deadlines are met under both normal (LO) and degraded (HI) operating modes. This theorem provides two separate conditions, one for each mode, that must both be satisfied.
steps: **Condition (A) - LO Mode Schedulability Check:**
For every relevant time interval `delta` (up to a pseudo-polynomial bound):
Calculate the total demand from all LO-criticality tasks using `dbf_LO_LO`.
Calculate the total demand from all HI-criticality tasks using `dbf_LO_HI` (which incorporates virtual deadlines).
Sum these demands. If `total_demand_LO_mode > delta` for any `delta`, the system is NOT schedulable.
**Condition (B) - HI Mode Schedulability Check:**
For every relevant time interval `delta` (up to a pseudo-polynomial bound):
Calculate the total demand from all LO-criticality tasks using `dbf_HI_LO` (which incorporates the admission control rate `r_i`).
Calculate the total demand from all HI-criticality tasks using `dbf_HI_HI` (which uses HI-WCETs and accounts for carry-over jobs).
Sum these demands. If `total_demand_HI_mode > delta` for any `delta`, the system is NOT schedulable.
If both Condition (A) and Condition (B) are satisfied, the system is deemed schedulable by EDF-GVD.
key_insights: Extends the classical EDF schedulability test to mixed-criticality systems by considering two distinct operational modes.
Each mode's demand calculation reflects the specific WCETs, deadlines (virtual or actual), and admission policies relevant to that mode.
The theorem provides a comprehensive framework for verifying the correctness of EDF-GVD schedules.

dependencies: lemma: Lemma 1: Classical EDF Schedulability Test

formal_description.statement: Let c be a constant such that c < 1 and sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} (C_i / T_i) + sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_LO_i / T_i) <= c. Then, Condition (A) is true for forall delta >= 0, if it is true for all delta such that delta < c_1 - c * max{ max_{tau_i in tau_LO} {T_i - D_i}, max_{tau_i in tau_HI} {T_i - D_v_i} }.

variables.c: An upper bound on the total utilization in LO mode
variables.U_LO_total: Total utilization in LO mode (sum of C_i/T_i for LO tasks and C_LO_i/T_i for HI tasks)
variables.D_v_i: Virtual deadline of HI-criticality task tau_i
variables.c_1: An undefined constant (as per paper's text)

assumptions: The total utilization in LO mode (U_LO_total) is strictly less than 1 (U_LO_total < 1)
Condition (A) of Theorem 1 is being checked
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a finite upper bound for the interval length delta that needs to be checked for Condition (A) of Theorem 1. If Condition (A) holds for all delta up to this bound, it holds for all delta, enabling a pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test.

informal_sketch.intuition: Checking schedulability for 'all delta >= 0' is impossible. This lemma states that if the total utilization in LO mode is less than 1, we only need to check a finite, bounded range of `delta` values. Beyond this range, if the system hasn't failed, it won't fail.
steps: Calculate the total utilization `U_LO_total` for LO mode (sum of `C_i/T_i` for LO tasks and `C_LO_i/T_i` for HI tasks).
Identify the maximum 'offset' or 'slack' terms for tasks in LO mode: `max_offset_LO = max(max_{tau_i in tau_LO} {T_i - D_i}, max_{tau_i in tau_HI} {T_i - D_v_i})`.
The lemma states that if Condition (A) holds for all `delta` up to a specific bound (which depends on `c_1`, `c`, and `max_offset_LO`), then it holds for all `delta`.
This bound is derived from the property that if utilization is less than 1, demand grows slower than time, so eventually, demand will not exceed time.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_delta_bound_A(task_set_LO, task_set_HI, c_1_val):
    U_LO_total = 0
    max_offset_LO = 0
    for tau_i_LO in task_set_LO:
        U_LO_total += tau_i_LO.C / tau_i_LO.T
        max_offset_LO = max(max_offset_LO, tau_i_LO.T - tau_i_LO.D)
    for tau_i_HI in task_set_HI:
        U_LO_total += tau_i_HI.C_LO / tau_i_HI.T
        max_offset_LO = max(max_offset_LO, tau_i_HI.T - tau_i_HI.D_v)
    
    if U_LO_total >= 1:
        return float('inf') # Schedulability not possible if utilization >= 1
    
    # The paper's formula for the bound is unusual and uses an undefined c_1.
    # A more standard form for such a bound is typically max_offset / (1 - U_total).
    # Adhering to the paper's stated formula:
    bound_delta = c_1_val - U_LO_total * max_offset_LO 
    return bound_delta
key_insights: Transforms an infinite number of checks into a finite, manageable number, making the schedulability test practical.
Relies on the property that if total utilization is below 1, the demand function's slope is less than 1, ensuring it eventually stays below the `delta` line.

dependencies: theorem: Theorem 1: MC Schedulability Test for EDF-GVD

formal_description.statement: Let c_1 and c_2 be two constants such that sum_{tau_i in tau_LO, r_i > 0} (r_i * C_i / T_i) <= c_1, sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_HI_i / T_i) <= c_2, and c_1 + c_2 < 1. Then, Condition (B) is true for forall delta >= 0, if it is true for all delta such that delta < (c_1 * max_{tau_i in tau_LO, r_i > 0} {T_i - D_i + T_i / r_i} + c_2 * max_{tau_i in tau_HI} {T_i - D_i + D_v_i}) / (1 - c_1 - c_2).

variables.c_1: An upper bound on the effective utilization of LO tasks in HI mode
variables.c_2: An upper bound on the utilization of HI tasks in HI mode

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a finite upper bound for the interval length delta that needs to be checked for Condition (B) of Theorem 1. If Condition (B) holds for all delta up to this bound, it holds for all delta, enabling a pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to Lemma 3, this lemma provides a finite upper bound for checking schedulability in HI mode. If the total effective utilization in HI mode (considering `r_i` for LO tasks and `C_HI_i` for HI tasks) is less than 1, then the demand function will eventually grow slower than time, guaranteeing schedulability beyond a certain point.
steps: Calculate the effective utilization for LO tasks in HI mode: `U_HI_LO_mode = sum_{tau_i in tau_LO, r_i > 0} (r_i * C_i / T_i)`.
Calculate the utilization for HI tasks in HI mode: `U_HI_HI_mode = sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_HI_i / T_i)`.

Identify the maximum 'offset' terms for both types of tasks in HI mode: `max_offset_LO_HI_mode = max_{tau_i in tau_LO, r_i > 0} {T_i - D_i + T_i / r_i}` and `max_offset_HI_HI_mode = max_{tau_i in tau_HI} {T_i - D_i + D_v_i}`.
The bound `bound_delta` is calculated using these utilizations and offsets. If Condition (B) holds for all `delta` up to this `bound_delta`, it holds for all `delta`.
key_insights: Provides a finite bound for checking HI mode schedulability, making the test practical.
The bound incorporates the unique demand characteristics of LO tasks under admission control and HI tasks with their pessimistic WCETs.

results.identifier: Theorem 2: Bound on Idle Time for HI-to-LO Mode Switch

formal_description.statement: Let t_d denote the absolute deadline of the latest HI-criticality job that overruns its LO-WCET in this HI mode. Then, there must be an idle time instant at or before t_d + L_1, where L_1 = (sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} C_LO_i + sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} (r_i * C_i)) / (1 - sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_LO_i / T_i) - sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} (r_i * C_i / T_i)).

variables.t_d: Absolute deadline of the latest HI-criticality job that overran its LO-WCET and triggered HI mode
variables.L_1: The maximum time duration from t_d until an idle time instant occurs
variables.r_i: Minimum cumulative admission rate for LO-criticality task tau_i

assumptions: The system is currently in HI mode

The total effective utilization (sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_LO_i / T_i) + sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} (r_i * C_i / T_i)) is strictly less than 1. This ensures the denominator is positive and an idle time will eventually occur.
formal_description.conclusion: Guarantees an upper bound (L_1) on the time duration from the deadline of the last overrunning HI-criticality job until the processor becomes idle. An idle time is a necessary precondition for the system to switch back to LO mode.

informal_sketch.intuition: Even in HI mode, if the overall system utilization (considering HI tasks at their C_LO_i and LO tasks at their guaranteed r_i rate) is less than 1, the processor cannot be continuously busy forever. This theorem provides a mathematical guarantee for when an idle period *must* occur, which is crucial for the system's ability to recover and switch back to LO mode.
steps: Assume, for contradiction, that the processor is continuously busy in the interval `[t_d, t_d + L_1)`.

Calculate the total work that *could* be executed by HI-criticality tasks in this interval, assuming they complete within their `C_LO_i` (as this bound is for returning to LO mode behavior): `sum_{tau_i in tau_HI} (C_LO_i * (L_1 / T_i + 2))`.

Calculate the total work that *could* be executed by LO-criticality tasks in this interval, based on their admission rate `r_i` and WCET `C_i` (using Lemma 2): `sum_{tau_i in tau_LO} (r_i * C_i * (L_1 / T_i + 2))`.
The total work `W` in `[t_d, t_d + L_1)` would be the sum of these two work components.
If the processor is continuously busy, `W` must be equal to `L_1`.
Substitute the expressions for `W` and simplify the inequality. This simplification leads to a contradiction (`L_1 < L_1`), thus proving that an idle time must occur within the specified bound.
The formula for `L_1` is derived from this contradiction, representing the maximum length of a busy interval.
key_insights: Provides a theoretical guarantee for system recovery by bounding the time until an idle period, which is a necessary condition for switching back to LO mode.

This is crucial for MC systems where mode switches are expected to occur and graceful degradation is a design goal, as it ensures the system doesn't get 'stuck' in HI mode indefinitely due to continuous busyness.
